column3: the profile contract: admissibility, answerability, and the basis of a particular value
column5: profiles.yaml ranked SOURCES and said nothing about the BASIS of a value. A modern-critical figure reprinted in a Catholic reference work arrived as traditional chronology because of the shelf it stood on, and the rule that actually decided several withdrawals -- that section 4.3's reporting licence is granted to Ussher by name and to nothing else -- existed only as a silence the corpus cited as if it were text.
column6: profiles.yaml carries an `admissibility` block: fifteen named basis classes, seven admissible and eight not; the two-question rule (is the SOURCE admissible, then is the BASIS OF THIS VALUE admissible) asked in that order and BEFORE rank; an `own_voice` clause saying publication context is not a basis; a `preservation` clause saying refusing a basis is not an instruction to delete; and one narrow, named `reporting_exceptions` entry for Ussher whose narrowness is machine-enforced. Plus an `answerability` block making answerable-vs-preserved an axis orthogonal to disposition.

The quotation and its point are also written into the event's subject note. A refusal to assign a date is not a date assertion: it is negative evidence, methodological testimony, and a reason a locus is undated.
column8: Howlett, "Biblical Chronology", CE vol. 3 (1908), opening of the section "Creation of the world": "At least 200 dates have been suggested, varying from 3483 to 6934 years B.C., all based on the supposition that the Bible enables us to settle the point. But it does nothing of the sort."

column8: Souvay, "Nahum": the lower limit "which a well-known inscription of Nabonidus permits us to fix at 607 or 606 B.C.", and the article discards Josephus and Nicephorus on that ground; Drum, "Psalms": Ps 73 "as Briggs surmises", Ps 82 "the Assyrian invasion of Tiglath-pileser III in 737 B.C."; "Israelites": Chanaan "about 2300 B.C.", which the claim's own note attributes to Sayce's Babylonian synchronism
column12: test_the_unreviewed_debt_is_bounded_and_named pins the count at 5, so a lane that adds a sixth has to say so
column13: YES -- these are the open cases
column14: Two reasons, both stated. (1) SCOPE: the final cold review names these as 'what this review found outside the surface', 'not repair-lane failures', and this lane's brief section 31 forbids population beyond the enumerated corrections. (2) A MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, not a guessed one. Three of the five are the SOLE claim of a NARROW composition unit -- Nah 2-3, Ps 73, Ps 82 -- and composition-unit scope selection runs BEFORE answerability, so preserving a narrow unit's last answerable claim leaves that unit still winning the scope contest and then answering nothing. Measured on a copy of the corpus: the maintainer's invariant that every verse resolve to NON-EMPTY chronology metadata SURVIVES (0 answers with neither assertions nor a note, over all 35,809 verses), but 74 verses change status. Ps 73:1-24 and Ps 82:1-19 (42 verses) fall to undated-in-tradition carrying the article's own note, which is honest. Nahum 2:1-3:19 (32 verses) fall to RESEARCH-PENDING, whose note reads 'no ranked source has been inspected for this locus yet' -- and that is FALSE: Souvay's 'Nahum' was inspected, and the ruling would be that its basis is inadmissible, which is a different fact and the opposite of a silence. Correcting Nahum truthfully therefore needs either a gap row saying what is actually the case or a wider Nahum unit, both of which are population this lane's brief forbids. That is a maintainer's decision, not a silent choice by this lane.
